newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SOCCER-WEAH BAN EXTENDED TO SIX GAMES, MILAN WEIGHS APPEAL.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-WEAH BAN EXTENDED TO SIX GAMES, MILAN WEIGHS APPEAL.

text.p: FIFA fair play ambassador George
Weah had a one-match ban for head-butting a Portuguese opponent
extended to six games on Monday.
AC Milan's Liberian striker was handed a six-match
suspension after a special investigation by UEFA into the
head-butting incident last month in Portugal.
UEFA had originally suspended Weah for one match while they
launched an inquiry into the incident which took place in the
players' tunnel after last month's European Cup Champions'
League match with Porto.
Weah admitted head-butting Portuguese defender Jorge Costa
and breaking his nose. Costa underwent surgery later and was
ruled out of action for three weeks.
Milan, in a brief statement, said the club and its player
had noted UEFA's ruling and would "make a decision as soon as
possible in respect to a possible appeal". According to UEFA, an
appeal must be lodged by Thursday.
Weah, last year's World, European and African Player of the
Year, has said previously he had been stupid to commit the
offence but claimed he had suffered racist provocation.
UEFA said in a statement that Weah's exemplary past record
had been taken into account, hinting that the six-match ban
could have been far heavier.
"The committee took into consideration George Weah's
particularly gentlemanly conduct on the pitch, e.g. only three
yellow cards in UEFA competitions during the last five years, as
confirmed by the Fair Play Award granted to him by FIFA," the
statement said.
Weah has already missed last week's Champions' League game
in which AC Milan went out of the European Cup after a shock
home defeat to Rosenborg Trondheim of Norway.
He will have to sit out the next five matches of UEFA
competition for which his team qualifies.
Weah said after the incident he was willing to apologise for
his action on condition that Costa accept he had made racist
taunts but the Portuguese defender refused the olive branch.
The Liberian, who spent several years in the French league
before moving to Italy, has long held a reputation as one of the
sport's gentlemen and one of its fairest, as well as one of its
finest, players.
